title: How 3-Way Switches Work: Travelers, Commons, and Troubleshooting (Ask This Old House)
summary: This This Old House episode presents a practical, hands-on explanation of how 3-way switches operate to control a light from two locations. The hosts introduce the need for a three-conductor cable (black, red, white), distinguish travelers from the common, and show how power in, a load out, and a continuous neutral path are arranged in a two-switch circuit. Through a box mockup and guided narration, they demonstrate wiring travelers to brass screws, the common connection point, and how the circuit is completed from either end to allow multi-location control. The segment also covers common pitfalls when adding or replacing a dimmer in a 3-way circuit, such as misidentifying wires or using a single-pole dimmer, and ends with troubleshooting tips and practical wiring heuristics.

sections.title: Intro and cutaway rationale
sections.description: The hosts discuss the goal of a cutaway to illustrate how three-way switches work when multiple locations control a single light, and note the challenge of opening a real switch to show internals, leading to a custom mockup.

sections.title: Single-pole circuit refresher
sections.description: A review of the basic two-wire circuit: power in (black) and neutral (white) feeding a load (light), with the switch completing or breaking the circuit to control the load.

sections.title: Three-way basics: introducing three-conductor cable and common vs travelers
sections.description: Introduces the need for a three-conductor cable between two 3-way switches and the distinction between traveler wires and the common (base point) on each switch.

sections.title: Wiring the 3-way in the box: travelers on brass, common on screws
sections.description: Shows how black and red are used as travelers on the brass screws and how the remaining conductor serves as the common, with each switch box containing a common for either feed or load.

sections.title: Path from two locations: how the circuit is completed or broken
sections.description: Explains that lighting control operates by completing or breaking the circuit at either switch, while the neutral path remains uninterrupted.

sections.title: Dimmer considerations and common miswiring
sections.description: Addresses common scenarios when adding or replacing dimmers in a 3-way circuit, including why a single-pole dimmer often cannot be used and how miswiring (mixing up common and travelers) leads to partial or nonfunctional operation.

sections.title: Best practices and recap
concepts: identify travelers as black and red
designate the remaining wire as common
sections.description: Concludes with practical tips: consistently use black and red as travelers, identify the remaining conductor as the common, and follow a straightforward approach to diagnose and fix 3-way wiring issues.
